paras.text: Ethical approval for this study was granted by the local ethics committee. Families were recruited via social media. Between July and November 2021, each child completed two 30‐minute online sessions. On average, these baseline (T1) sessions were completed a week apart (M: 7 days). Time two (T2) assessment occurred between May and August 2022, when children completed a single online session. Assessment occurred during school holidays, over weekends or after school/preschool. The average time between T1 and T2 assessment was 282 days (range: 198–376). At both times, a parent questionnaire gathered information on children's social, emotional and self‐regulatory behaviour. After each assessment wave children received a digital gift card and certificate to thank them for participating. Data and anonymised protocol documents are available on the OSF platform. The Flanker and Advanced DCCS, were created and hosted on Gorilla Experiment Builder (www.gorilla.sc), while the Animal Race, Picture Naming and Matrix Reasoning tasks were adapted for online administration and presented using Microsoft PowerPoint. Due to technical difficulties, the order of the T1 session was reversed with four participants.

A child's age at school‐entry is typically determined by where their birthday falls relative to the nationally legislated school‐entry cut‐off (Verachtert et al. 2010). Since most countries have a single annual intake, children can be as much as a year older than the youngest members of their school cohort. While this is common practice, it has been argued that these early maturational differences can place the youngest students in a cohort at a disadvantage relative to their peers, having both short‐term and longer‐term implications on a child's experience and attitude towards school (e.g., Jeronimus et al. 2015). When a child's date of birth falls on the cusp of this cut‐off, some countries allow parents to decide whether to enroll a child in formal schooling when first eligible, or delay their entry until the following academic year. In recent years, several countries, including the United Kingdom, have seen an increase in the number of parents delaying children's primary school‐entry (King and Hammond 2021; Larsen et al. 2021; Scottish Government 2020a), also known as deferral. While parents’ reasons for deferral vary, research indicates that additional time in a play‐based learning environment is perceived to nurture important socio‐emotional skills which support learning and wellbeing (Simpson et al. 2024). Yet literature which might be drawn on to evaluate outcomes associated with a child's school‐entry age, and the implications for deferral, does not always account for both cognitive and socio‐emotional factors. Moreover, this research can be difficult to synthesise, since the effects of age and schooling are often studied in isolation. To address this, the present study used a longitudinal design to investigate both schooling‐ and age‐effects on regulatory processes underlying children's cognitive and socio‐emotional functioning. In doing so, we aim to contribute to discussions regarding school‐entry age, how it might interact with children's development, and the implications for school‐entry deferral.

Proponents of a younger school entry argue that the school environment offers valuable enrichment, providing children with a head start to learning (e.g., Bingham and Whitebread 2018). Conversely, early exposure to formal curricula could increase anxiety and negatively affect a child's self‐esteem and motivation to learn (e.g., Sharp 2002). Indeed, advocates of a later school‐entry argue that extended informal play‐based education fosters important cognitive and socio‐emotional skills (e.g., Singer et al. 2006; Vogt et al. 2018), allowing children to acquire skills more efficiently (Suggate 2015) with positive longer‐term effects on self‐esteem and academic self‐belief (Givord 2020). Thus, to assess the impact of school‐entry age on development and wellbeing, a “whole‐child” approach is needed, evaluating cognitive, behavioural and socio‐emotional functioning (Sylva et al. 2020).

paras.sec_title: Predictors of School Readiness and Engagement
paras.text: Over the last two decades, there has been greater recognition of the importance of a child's regulatory and socio‐emotional skills for school (e.g., Denham et al. 2014; Sylva et al. 2020). Self‐regulation refers to an individual's capacity to manage and modulate cognition, emotion and behaviour in response to environmental demands and goals (Bailey and Jones 2019). Since cognition and emotion work together to organise thought and action (Cantor et al. 2019), difficulties with self‐regulation can both impede learning and influence social interactions with peers and teachers, ultimately affecting a child's sense of belonging, acceptance and attitude towards school (Denham et al. 2014). Critically, these early school experiences have the potential to influence future academic engagement and performance (Immordino‐Yang and Damasio 2007; Meyer and Turner 2006).

paras.sec_title: Predictors of School Readiness and Engagement
paras.text: Self‐regulation relies on a set of higher‐order cognitive processes, defined in psychological literature as executive function (EF) or cognitive control (Miller and Cohen 2001). EF is generally agreed to comprise three partially dissociable cognitive processes (Ibbotson 2023), including inhibitory control, the ability to inhibit goal‐irrelevant impulses; working memory (WM), the capacity to keep task‐relevant information in mind; and cognitive flexibility, the ability to shift between tasks or mental operations (e.g., Carlson et al. 2013). These domain‐general processes support a wide range of skills, including cognitive, emotional and social functions (Bailey and Jones 2019). For instance, children rely on inhibitory control in social situations, such as refraining from hitting another child when provoked, but also when filtering out classroom distractions to focus on a prescribed task.

paras.sec_title: Predictors of School Readiness and Engagement
paras.text: EF is consistently recognised as a key predictor of school readiness and academic success (e.g., Blair and Razza 2007; Turnbull et al. 2024). Children who enter school with more developed EF exhibit superior regulatory skills, allowing them to effectively manage their attention, behaviour and emotions (e.g., Bailey and Jones 2019; Diamond 2013). These skills are crucial for navigating the multifaceted demands of the school environment, and are foundational for academic achievement, as they empower children to engage more fully in learning activities, interact positively with peers and teachers, and adapt to new challenges and routines (Bailey and Jones 2019). Furthermore, emerging EF is useful for comparing cognition and regulatory skills among children from different school cohorts, especially in early schooling years when academic exposure varies.

Age‐related enhancements to EF, including increased WM capacity, improved focus on task‐relevant information (cognitive flexibility) and inhibition of task‐irrelevant information (Carlson et al. 2013), enable more sophisticated cognition. Since the brain networks supporting EF only reach full maturation in early adulthood (Gogtay et al. 2004), maturational considerations are crucial to discussions related to school‐entry age. As neural connectivity becomes more efficient with age and experience, relatively older children may exhibit more sophisticated and efficient cognition, including greater EF (e.g., Luna et al. 2004; Wenger and Lövdén 2016). Indeed, during the early years of school, research consistently finds that older children demonstrate more favourable cognitive and academic outcomes (e.g., Allhusen et al. 2007; Fortner and Jenkins 2017; Larsen et al. 2021), and socio‐emotional skills and behaviour (e.g., Datar and Gottfried 2015; Dee and Sievertsen 2018) relative to younger peers. Yet maturational processes do not work in isolation, and wider features of their environment, such as parenting practices, the educational setting and peer influence, simultaneously influence development (Bronfenbrenner 2005). For this reason, some stakeholders propose an earlier school‐entry to stimulate cognitive development and mitigate disparities in the home learning environment (e.g., Bingham and Whitebread 2018; Stipek 2002). Given that maturational and environmental factors interact, both need to be accounted for in research which might inform educational policy and practices related to school‐entry age.

Research investigating EF development across the transition to school has examined the effects of the educational environment by keeping age constant. Assessing children born either side of the school‐entry cut‐off (Figure 1a), researchers aim to isolate maturational processes (at baseline) before educational paths diverge (Morrison et al. 2019). Longitudinal assessment then tracks how outcomes change as a function of the educational setting (preschool vs. school entry), known as schooling effects (Morrison et al. 2019). Using this approach, schooling effects in EF have been reported in German (baseline age: 5.5yrs, Brod et al. 2017) and Scottish (baseline age: 4.5yrs, Davidson et al. 2023; McKay et al. 2022) samples, although results were not always consistent. German children who spent the year in primary school demonstrated larger improvements in cognitive flexibility accuracy relative to peers who remained in preschool (Brod et al. 2017), but this was not replicated in the Scottish sample despite using the same task (McKay et al. 2022). However, Scottish school entrants demonstrated larger improvements in visual WM development relative to same‐aged peers who remained in preschool (Davidson et al. 2023), not assessed in the German sample. Further research is therefore needed to clarify the impact of schooling on different domains of EF.

While the formal school environment undoubtedly stimulates cognitive development over‐and‐above maturation, this research fails to address how the youngest children in a cohort manage the cognitive, social and emotional demands of school relative to the oldest. To explore this, researchers would need to recruit children within a particular educational cohort (Figure 1a), such as Grade 1, to evaluate how age influences participant outcomes across time, also known as relative‐age effects. Yet there is a notable lack of literature investigating relative‐age effects in EF, as it is generally studied across wider age bands to capture broader trends in EF development. Within existing research, one study investigating EF differentiation with a preschool sample (aged 3–4years) found that age effects in EF were present when contrasting outcomes across narrow, six‐month age intervals. However, another study evaluating EF with a sample of fifth graders, did not find relative‐age effects in their EF outcomes, although the oldest cohort members demonstrated a greater willingness to exert cognitive effort relative to younger peers (Radl and Valdés 2024).

Much research investigating relative‐age effects with school entrants has instead focused on academic outcomes, which consistently indicates that age effects are largest early in schooling (e.g., Allhusen et al. 2007; Fortner and Jenkins 2017). While some authors find that academic age effects diminish (e.g., Lubotsky and Kaestner 2016; Vestheim et al. 2019) and even disappear by the end of the primary years (Larsen et al. 2021), others report enduring effects in secondary school (McPhillips and Jordan‐Black 2009; Ponzo and Scoppa 2014) and beyond (Crawford et al. 2010; Kawaguchi 2011). In other domains, relative‐age effects appear to manifest in attentional and self‐regulatory difficulties during primary schooling (e.g., Dee and Sievertsen 2018), while peer and emotional problems are more common in early adolescence (e.g., Broughton et al. 2023; Patalay et al. 2015), although other studies do not find relative‐age effects in socio‐emotional skills (e.g., Allhusen et al. 2007). Critically, since EF (primary outcome) underlies many of these skills, EF could feasibly drive these academic and socio‐emotional age effects (secondary outcome) during the early years of school.

A child's age at school‐entry may impact their development and wellbeing, especially those born on the cusp of the school‐entry cut‐off, making them one of the youngest in their cohort. While primary schooling is known to enhance children's neurocognitive development relative to similar‐aged peers who remain in pre‐school (schooling effect), less is known about these children's development relative to older cohort members (age effect). Prior research has predominantly focused on how school entry‐age influences academic performance, but a notable research gap remains regarding children's EF and socio‐emotional development. To address this, our study targeted a unique sample of children within Scotland who were eligible to delay school‐entry based on their birth date. At the time of conducting this study, Scottish legislation entitled families with a child born in the months of January and February (up to two months prior to the school‐entry cut‐off) automatic eligibility to defer their child's school‐entry and receive an additional year of funded preschool education (Scottish Government 2020a). Targeting three distinct groups (Figure 1b), we used Latent Change Score (LCS) models, in two separate contrasts, to evaluate how the deferral decision interacted with EF development and parent‐reported socio‐emotional and regulatory functioning, over the academic year. The value of this analytic approach is that it allows us to assess individual gains using latent difference scores, capturing the relationship between initial and later performance. Additionally, the model allows us to simultaneously model group‐level change, and individual variance in change, across this period (Kievit et al. 2018). Importantly, this analytic approach assists in mitigating potential confounds by focusing on changes within individuals over time, rather than exclusive focus on between‐individual differences. This is particularly relevant within the current sample, given that preschool closures during the COVID‐19 pandemic (in the period prior to the current study) are likely to have influenced children's learning, socialisation and development (Hardie et al. 2026).

In our first contrast, we examined schooling effects among children of the same age who either entered school when first eligible (Non‐deferred P1s), or spent an additional year in preschool (Deferred Pre‐schoolers). We anticipated comparable EF scores at baseline, reflecting maturational similarities in cognition (Brod et al. 2017; Davidson et al. 2023; McKay et al. 2022). In contrast, we expected the Non‐deferred P1 group to achieve better baseline scores on socio‐emotional and self‐regulatory outcomes, as parents electing to send a child to school when first eligible might view them as possessing more mature socio‐emotional skills (Simpson et al. 2024). By the academic year's end, we expected both groups to show improved EF, with Non‐deferred P1s making larger gains due to the cognitive and attentional demands of formal education and explored whether this would vary across EF domains. Furthermore, the Deferred Preschool group was expected to demonstrate a larger improvement in parent‐reported socio‐emotional and regulatory skills, given the emphasis typically placed on socio‐emotional skills within a play‐based preschool setting (e.g., Singer et al. 2006).

Our second contrast investigated age effects among Primary 1 entrants born approximately a year apart (Deferred P1s vs. Non‐deferred P1s). We expected the Deferred P1 group to demonstrate more mature EF at baseline due to age‐related differences in cognitive maturation (Howard et al. 2015). No differences were anticipated in socio‐emotional and regulatory functioning, as we hypothesised that Non‐deferred entrants might exhibit mature socio‐emotional skills for children their age (Simpson et al. 2024). At the end of the academic year, we expected EF to improve in both groups, and explored whether the rate of improvement might be accelerated among Non‐deferred P1s (catch‐up effect) or whether any baseline age effect would persist over time. No group differences were expected in socio‐emotional and self‐regulatory scores.

Families were recruited from across Scotland. Due to difficulties recruiting the Non‐deferred P1 Group, eligibility criteria were extended to include children born in November and December 2015/2016. The final sample included children born between November 2015–February 2016 (Deferred P1), and children born between November 2016–February 2017 (Non‐deferred P1 and Deferred Preschool). One hundred and eighteen children took part in at least one assessment at the initial time point (T1). Eight of these children did not participate in the second assessment point (6.8% attrition), and while demographically representative of the full sample, this group achieved lower scores on T1 WM, Vocabulary and Nonverbal Reasoning relative to the final sample (see Table S1 for details of the excluded participants). The final sample included a total of 110 children (47% female). Most participants were White, which is broadly representative of Scottish demographics. Group‐level descriptive statistics are presented in Table 1. Most families (68%) resided in areas classified as the least deprived in Scotland (Quintiles 4 to 5 of the Scottish Index of Multiple Deprivation, Scottish Government 2020b), and the majority of reporting parents (98% mothers) had obtained a university degree (highest level: 45% undergraduate, 42% postgraduate). Neighbourhood deprivation, a proxy for socio‐economic status (Jerrim 2024), was comparable across groups (Table 1). One child had received a diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), and another two were awaiting assessment for ASD. These children were included in all cognitive analyses as their scores were comparable with scores within their group, however, two of them were excluded from the socio‐emotional analyses due to outlying scores (see Table S2 for additional information related to missing data).

A child‐friendly adaptation of the Eriksen flanker task (Eriksen and Eriksen 1974) evaluated inhibitory control. The game was introduced as a game of tag with Nemo. Participants “caught Nemo” by pushing the keyboard button which corresponded with the direction he was swimming (left: X‐key, right: M‐key; stickers were placed on these keys to help children locate them with ease). Children were warned to be careful because Nemo (central fish) would sometimes try to trick them by swimming in the opposite direction from his friends (incongruent trials).

Overall participant accuracy was high, most children achieved an accuracy rate of 90% or higher1, a common effect in middle childhood (e.g., Willoughby et al. 2023). For this reason, RT was likely to capture greater variance in participant data and chosen as the primary measure of inhibitory control. Further, since raw RT and difference scores (such as the congruency effect) increase error variance and fare poorly in Structural Equation Modelling, we chose to focus analyses on incongruent log RT (see review by Yangüez et al. 2024).

The DCCS was included as a measure of cognitive flexibility (adapted from Zelazo 2006). On participants’ screens an image of a blue bunny was presented at the bottom left and a red car at the bottom right (Figure 2b). Participants had to match a centrally presented target with one of the bottom pictures according to a prescribed dimension (colour or shape). On colour trials a blue target corresponded with the X‐key and a red target corresponded with the M‐key, and on shape trials the X‐key was used to select the bunny‐shape, and the M‐key was used to select the car‐shape. Critically, the colour of the target (red bunny or blue car) was never congruent with the images visible at the bottom of the screen.

Adapted from Majerus et al. (2006), the Animal Race assessed participants’ verbal WM. Children were told that seven (single syllable) farm animals were taking part in a series of races, including cow, dog, goat, hen, horse, pig and sheep (Figure 2c). Participants listened to the announcer stating the order in which the animals crossed the finish line (participant screens only showed the podium/set‐size during the announcement). Once the race was complete, the animals who had competed would appear on their screen (animals always appeared in their designated lanes), and the child was required to repeat the finishing order to the experimenter, who would arrange the animals on the podium for the child to verify. After initial instructions, participants completed two practice trials in which two animals were racing (set‐size = 2). If participants responded incorrectly to any of these items, feedback was provided and the instructions repeated. Test trials started with a set‐size of two to a maximum of seven. Three trials were presented in each set‐size, however children, were automatically credited with the third trial after correct responses to the first two trials in a given set‐size. Feedback was not explicitly provided to participants during assessed trials, and the task was discontinued after a child achieved a score of 0 on all three trials in a set‐size. Scores were calculated by summing the total number of animals remembered within correct (or credited) trials (a correct response on a set‐size of two was awarded 2‐points, while a correct response on a set‐size of four was awarded 4‐points).

The Picture Naming subtest of the Weschler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence (WPPSI‐III; Wechsler 2002) was used as a measure of expressive vocabulary and language development. Participants named the object depicted in the image, for example, star, guitar. Administration began at the age‐appropriate starting point (item 7) and the reverse rule applied if they failed to provide the correct response to either item 7 or 8. The task was discontinued after five consecutive incorrect responses, and 1‐point assigned to every correct response (max score: 30). Raw scores were standardised based on the participant's age.

The Matrix Reasoning subtest of the WPPSI‐III (Wechsler 2002) assessed non‐verbal reasoning. Participants were required to select one of a possible four or five pictures to complete a visual matrix or pattern. After administering three sample items, testing began at the age‐appropriate starting point (4yos: item 1; 5yos: item 5). The reverse rule was applied if a 5‐year‐old participant failed to provide the correct response to item 5 or 6. The task was discontinued after four consecutive incorrect responses or four incorrect responses on five consecutive items. 1‐point was assigned to every correct response (max score: 29). Raw scores were standardised based on the participant's age.

The CSBQ consists of 34 items, on which parents rate a child's behaviour using a 5‐point scale (Not True to Very True) (Howard and Melhuish 2017). Subscales assessing socio‐emotional problems (higher scores reflect poorer outcomes) included externalising (5‐items, e.g., ‘show wide mood swings’) and internalising behaviour (5‐items, e.g., ‘most days says feeling unwell’). Subscales assessing self‐regulatory and socio‐emotional strengths (lower scores reflect poorer outcomes) included sociability (7‐items, e.g., ‘plays easily with other children’), prosocial behaviour (5‐items, e.g., ‘happy to share’), behavioural self‐regulation (6‐items, e.g., ‘not able to sit still when necessary’), cognitive self‐regulation (5‐items, e.g., ‘persists with tasks until completed’), and emotional self‐regulation (6‐items, e.g., ‘gets over being upset quickly’). Subscales are reported to have good reliability (α‐range: 0.74 to 0.89), and show convergent validity with the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) (Howard and Melhuish 2017). Internal consistency (α) in our subscales ranged between 0.65 and 0.83 (details provided in Table S3), with the exception of the T1 internalising subscale which was 0.49 and therefore dropped from further analyses.

Data were analysed using R Statistical Software (v4.3.2; R Core R Core Team 2023). Raw data from the Flanker and DCCS was pre‐processed (see Table S4 for details of exclusions by task and time) to remove any responses less than 200 ms and participant accuracy calculated based on the remaining trials. Inaccurate trials and trials over 10 seconds were removed from the data. Outliers were removed from each participant's data, identified as any trials in which a participant's RT was three standard deviations above their mean, and led to the exclusion of 0.42% to 2.63% of trials (details in Table S4). Participant RT was calculated for each condition of each task, and then log‐transformed to correct for skew (for the sake of clarity, back‐transformed RTs are reported in Table 2). When participant accuracy was less than or equivalent to chance (50% or less), their data was excluded from that particular task (see Table S2 for exclusions).

Longitudinal change in participant outcomes was modelled using univariate LCS models (Figure 3, Kievit et al. 2018). Kievit and colleagues (Kievit et al. 2018) recommend that sample size be considered alongside other factors, such as indicator reliability, when evaluating whether there is sufficient statistical power to detect effects. Further, LCS models have been effectively used in research on related topics with a comparable sample size, with group sizes ranging between 30 and 39 (Davidson et al. 2023; McKay et al. 2022).

Models of verbal WM (Total Animals correct), inhibitory control (Flanker Incongruent RT), cognitive flexibility (DCCS Mixed Block RT) and the CSBQ composite are reported in the results sections. Models for the Flanker Congruent trials and DCCS Single Block trials are reported in supplementary material (Table S8). Separate analyses were conducted to investigate the effects of (1) Schooling (Nondef‐P1 vs. Def‐PreS), and (2) Age (Def‐P1 vs. Nondef‐P1), with the aforementioned covariates (cov) included in our models. Multi‐group models allowed parameter estimates to vary by group and enabled later group comparison. Parameters of interest included: baseline (T1) scores (xT1), variance in baseline scores (σ2xT1, within‐group variability in baseline scores), change scores (Δx, a latent difference score, reflecting difference between T1 and T2 scores), variance in the change scores (σ2Δx, within‐group variability in change scores) and the self‐feedback parameter (βxT1Δx, the extent to which change is dependent on T1 scores) (Kievit et al. 2018). Negative change scores reflect improved performance in RT outcomes (faster RT at T2 relative to T1) and positive changes scores reflect improved performance on the WM subtest and the CSBQ composite.

Models were set‐up using the Lavaan package (v0.6.16; Rosseel 2012). Full information maximum likelihood was used for model estimation and to account for missing data (details provided in Table S2). Since we were limited to two waves of data collection, our models were just‐identified, that is, there were as many unique pieces of information entered into the model as parameters that were estimated. Thus, to evaluate whether group outcomes differed significantly, parameters of interest were constrained to be equal across groups. The change in model fit, assessed using likelihood ratio testing (a chi‐square difference test), was used to contrast the constrained model to the just‐identified model (freely estimated for each group). When model constraint led to a worsening of model fit (p < 0.05), this indicated that significant group differences were evident in the constrained parameter (Kievit et al. 2018). Additionally, we report the relative Akaike weights of the free and constrained model (calculated as AIC weight of free model divided by the AIC weight of the constrained model (Wagenmakers and Farrell 2004), indicating how likely the free model is relative to the constrained model (Kievit et al. 2018). For instance, a ratio of 2 would suggest that the free model is two times more likely to occur than the constrained model.

Group‐level descriptive statistics of gender, age, vocabulary and reasoning are presented in Table 1, and group averages for EF and CSBQ outcomes are presented in Table 2. Consistent with other developmental research (e.g., Roebers 2022), high accuracy on the Flanker and DCCS meant that RT was a better indicator of EF ability in our sample. Overall, children were slower on trials with greater cognitive conflict (Incongruent > Congruent; Mixed > Single, see Table S9). Group averages for the CSBQ subscales fell within the expected range for pre‐schoolers (Early Start n.d.).

Consistent with previous research (Brod et al. 2017; Davidson et al. 2023; McKay et al. 2022), we found that children of a similar age (Non‐deferred P1 and Deferred Preschool groups) demonstrated statistically comparable EF at the beginning of the academic year. At the end of the year, a schooling effect was found in verbal WM, but not other EF domains. This finding is consistent with recent research by Davidson et al. (2023), who reported a schooling effect in visuo‐spatial WM, and work by Finch (2019), which highlights the unique opportunities provided within the school environment to practice and enhance WM. On the other EF tasks, groups demonstrated comparable gains in inhibitory control and cognitive flexibility. Although using different tasks and outcomes (accuracy), previous studies (Brod et al. 2017; McKay et al. 2022) also failed to find a schooling effect in inhibitory control and outcomes have been inconsistent on tasks assessing cognitive flexibility. This could indicate that these EF domains are less susceptible to the effects of schooling, and within the current sample at least, enhancements to inhibitory control appear to follow a maturational timetable, meaning that improvement is more closely aligned with age than features of the educational environment.

Overall, the schooling effect that we found in verbal WM highlights that there are certain cognitive benefits associated with entering school when first eligible. Yet, we also observed that after deferring, children entered school with greater verbal WM and inhibitory control relative to the youngest members of their school cohort, likely due to their age, rather than additional time spent in preschool. However, during the first year at school, the age advantage in verbal WM already appeared to wane, perhaps due to the fact that schooling boosts WM development, although, the age advantage in inhibitory control endured. While this finding needs replication, a persistent age effect in inhibitory control could underlie the early academic advantage held by older cohort members (e.g., Allhusen et al. 2007; Fortner and Jenkins 2017), but as we did not assess academic outcomes, our data do not speak to this issue.

paras.sec_title: Effect of Deferral on Parent‐Reported Socio‐Emotional and Self‐Regulatory Development
paras.text: When examining parent‐reported socio‐emotional and self‐regulatory skills, we found that the Deferred and Non‐deferred P1 groups achieved statistically comparable outcomes at the beginning and end of the school year. However, a different picture emerged when contrasting outcomes within our younger groups. Consistent with recent research (Simpson et al. 2024), parents were more likely to report poorer socio‐emotional and regulatory outcomes when electing to delay their four‐and‐a‐half‐year‐olds school‐entry (Deferred Pre‐schooler), compared to those who sent their child to school when first eligible (Non‐deferred P1). However, at the end of the year, the CSBQ composite was comparable across groups, suggestive of a catch‐up effect within the preschool group. Overall, results indicate that these gains were largest amongst those who achieved poorer baseline scores within the group.

paras.sec_title: Effect of Deferral on Parent‐Reported Socio‐Emotional and Self‐Regulatory Development
paras.text: These findings suggest that the deferral year might provide certain children with additional time to develop important socio‐emotional and self‐regulatory skills, which could potentially positively influence their school experience and engagement when transitioning to school the following year. For instance, inefficient emotional regulation has been found to prevent a child from applying higher order cognitive processes (EF) in the classroom (Blair 2002), while poorer social skills could alienate peers and negatively affect a child's self‐esteem and attitude towards school (Denham et al. 2014). On the other hand, the socio‐emotional benefit of deferral may be less obvious for those children whose parents perceived them to possess well‐developed socio‐emotional and self‐regulatory skills at baseline. Although, it is possible that these children made socio‐emotional gains in outcomes not directly assessed in our study, such as improved self‐esteem.

paras.sec_title: Effect of Deferral on Parent‐Reported Socio‐Emotional and Self‐Regulatory Development
paras.text: Critically, the socio‐emotional benefits of deferral ought to be interpreted as a reflection of parental opinion. This is due to the bias inherent in parental report (e.g., Zapolski and Smith 2013). Specifically, while the deferral year might indeed be associated with enhancements to socio‐emotional and regulatory skills, it is also possible that parents’ CSBQ ratings are influenced by their views of deferral. Although, EF gains made during the deferral year are likely to support children's socio‐emotional development (Hughes and Ensor 2011). For instance, improvements to inhibitory control are likely to influence a child's capacity to regulate their emotions and behaviour (e.g., Rhoades et al. 2009). For this reason, these findings need replication using more objective measures of socio‐emotional and self‐regulatory skills.

Longitudinal research has the benefit of tracking developmental change across time; and while our study was limited to two assessment points, the inclusion of three groups was novel as it enabled us to address the topic from different perspectives and account for the interaction between schooling and maturation. Additionally, we adopted a “whole child” approach to the debate of school‐entry age by assessing regulatory processes underlying both cognitive and socio‐emotional skills, identified as important considerations to parents navigating deferral (Simpson et al. 2024).

Since data collection coincided with the COVID‐19 pandemic, our study was adapted for online administration. Although pre/schools remained open throughout our study, the closure of early education centres between March 2020 and February 2021 likely impacted children's socialisation, learning and development (e.g., Hardie et al. 2026). Notably, all participants were likely affected by these circumstances, albeit in different ways, such as through differential access to early education centres, educational resources and opportunities within the home environment, or the quantity and quality of time spend with caregivers and/or siblings. Group‐level analysis using LCS models aimed to mitigate confounds arising from individual variation in these, and other contextual factors. A notable limitation of our study was our sample size. While our group size was comparable with previous research (Brod et al. 2017; McKay et al. 2022), a larger sample may have given us greater statistical power to detect effects. While remote assessment enabled us to recruit families from across Scotland, it is likely that needing access to a computer with a stable internet connection excluded certain families from participating. Linked to this, our demographics were skewed towards families living in areas classified as the least deprived in Scotland. While, this is representative of the parents which elect to defer (Scottish Government 2020a), this recruitment bias may partly explain why it was harder to recruit Non‐deferred entrants. Yet, the advantage of this is that our groups were demographically comparable, and therefore while our data may not address socio‐economic differences associated with deferral, the reported differences across groups cannot be solely attributed to demographic confounds. As previously mentioned, there are limitations in relying exclusively on parental report when assessing self‐regulatory and socio‐emotional outcomes (e.g., Zapolski and Smith 2013). Inclusion of tasks which may more objectively assess socio‐emotional functioning would be a viable alternative to parent report. Future studies could potentially overcome this and other limitations, including biases in sample demographics and shortened assessment batteries, by conducting research within the preschool and primary school settings. Additionally, with a larger sample, the relationship between socio‐emotional gains and EF development could be explored in the future.
